title: Python List
body:
Python's built-in sequence type. **[[List]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] is the
[[Abstract Data Type]]; this is the concrete thing the course actually uses**, with the
[[Implementation]] hidden. That note already says so, and this is the other end of the handoff.

```python
scores = [88, 92, 71]
scores[0]        # 88
scores[-1]       # 71, counting from the right
scores[1:3]      # [92, 71], a slice
scores.append(65)
len(scores)      # 4
```

## What differs from a C array

| | [[Array]] (C) | Python list |
|---|---|---|
| Size | fixed at declaration | grows and shrinks |
| Element types | all the same | anything, mixed |
| Bounds check | none; past the end is undefined behaviour | `IndexError`, immediately |
| Negative index | reads whatever is in memory | counts from the right |
| Slicing | write the loop yourself | `[a:b]` |

The bounds check is the difference worth dwelling on. In C, running off the end of an array
reads memory that belongs to something else, and the program keeps going with a wrong number or
corrupts something and crashes later. Python raises an `IndexError` on the spot. **The C version
is faster and the Python version is the reason you are learning here first.** See
[[Index]] and [[Runtime Errors]].

Negative indexing and slicing are pure convenience, and they are the two things that make list
code short enough to read.

## Mutability

A list can be changed in place, and this is the first place aliasing appears:

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a          # not a copy; both names refer to the same list
b.append(4)
print(a)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

`b = a[:]` copies. The distinction is [[Call by reference]] against [[Call by value]] in
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]], arriving a year early and without the pointer syntax to
explain it, and it is worth recognising as the same idea when [[Pointer]] shows up.

Iterating is what block 4's loops are for, and Python's `for` walks the elements directly rather
than counting to a length:

```python
for score in scores:
    total += score
```

What any of this **costs** (why `append` is cheap and inserting at the front is not) is
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]'s question, not this course's. See [[Time Complexity]].
